title: Martin Fowler, Software Architecture Guide
text:
## What Software Architecture Is

Martin Fowler frames architecture through Ralph Johnson's definition: architecture is about the important stuff, whatever that is. It is the shared understanding that expert developers hold about a system's design. Johnson criticizes the naive early-decisions framing and argues architecture is the set of decisions you wish you could get right early in a project, not necessarily the decisions made first, but the ones with the most lasting consequences and that are hardest to change later.

## Architecture Is Intertwined With Programming

Fowler stresses that good architecture is something that supports its own evolution and is deeply intertwined with programming. Architecture is not a separate phase or an ivory-tower artifact handed down to coders; it is embedded in the code itself. The job of identifying which elements are architecturally significant, the pieces where getting it wrong causes serious problems, is central to acting as an architect.

## Why Architecture Matters: Internal Quality and Cruft

Poor architecture generates cruft, the elements of the software that impede developers' ability to understand it. Cruft slows feature delivery and increases defects, making the software much harder to modify. Fowler's central and counter-intuitive claim is that high internal quality leads to faster delivery of new features. This reverses the common assumption that quality trades off against speed. While teams can sacrifice internal quality for short-term speed, cruft accumulates quickly, and experienced developers find that attention to internal quality pays off in weeks, not months, and certainly not years. The cost-of-change argument is the economic core of why a technical lead invests in architecture: the value of good design is that it keeps the cost of future change low.

title: Martin Fowler, Technical Debt Quadrant
text:
## The Debt Metaphor as a Communication Tool

Martin Fowler's Technical Debt Quadrant reframes the perennial argument over what counts as technical debt. Rather than debating whether messy code qualifies as debt, Fowler asks whether the debt metaphor is helpful for thinking about how to deal with design problems. Its value is in communicating design trade-offs to non-technical stakeholders, because everyone understands that debt yields short-term leverage but accrues interest that must eventually be paid.

## Two Axes, Four Quadrants

The quadrant separates debt along two axes: Reckless versus Prudent, and Deliberate versus Inadvertent.

Deliberate and Reckless: a team knowingly cuts corners believing speed beats design quality. Fowler argues this underestimates where the design payoff line sits, since clean code actually accelerates delivery, so the supposed speed is often illusory.

Deliberate and Prudent: a conscious short-term compromise taken to hit a release, where the debt yields value sooner but needs to be paid off as soon as possible. This is legitimate, managed debt.

Inadvertent and Reckless: messy code produced by teams ignorant of good design practices, leading to crippling interest payments or a long period of paying down the principal.

Inadvertent and Prudent: design flaws discovered only after deeper understanding of the project emerges. Fowler calls this inevitable even for teams that are excellent designers, because while you are programming you are learning, and you often only realize the right design after you have built the wrong one.

## Key Insight

The most useful distinction is prudent versus reckless, not debt versus non-debt. Even the best teams accumulate inadvertent debt as their knowledge of the domain evolves, so the goal is not zero debt but deliberate, prudent management of it.

title: Martin Fowler, MonolithFirst
text:
## The Recommendation

Martin Fowler argues you should not start a new project with microservices, even if you are sure your application will be big enough to make it worthwhile. Empirically, nearly all the successful microservices stories he has seen started with a monolith that grew too big and was broken up, and nearly all the cases where a system was built as microservices from scratch ended up in serious trouble.

## Two Reasons

First, YAGNI and feedback speed. When you launch a new application, you do not yet know if it will be useful. Microservices carry a significant MicroservicePremium, the operational overhead of managing many services, which slows the fast feedback cycles you most need while validating the product.

Second, bounded-context discovery. Any refactoring of functionality between services is much harder than it is in a monolith. Getting service boundaries right is very hard even for skilled architects, and premature boundaries are costly to move. Building a monolith first lets a team figure out what the right boundaries are before a microservices design brushes a layer of treacle over them.

## Implementation Paths

Fowler describes several approaches: designing a modular monolith up front (rarely done well), gradually peeling edge services off a core monolith, replacing the whole thing via SacrificialArchitecture once you understand the domain, or starting with a few coarse-grained services and refining boundaries progressively. The through-line is that stable boundaries are earned through domain understanding, not guessed at the outset.

title: Martin Fowler, StranglerFigApplication
text:
## The Metaphor

Martin Fowler named this pattern after the strangler fig vines he saw in Queensland in 2001. The fig germinates in the upper branches of a host tree and gradually grows down to the ground, drawing nutrients until the host tree dies, leaving the fig as an echo of its shape. This mirrors how to modernize a legacy system: grow a new system gradually around the edges of the old one, letting it take over, rather than replacing everything at once.

## The Problem With Big-Bang Rewrites

Legacy systems accumulate decades of patches and become hard to modify. A full replacement sounds straightforward, but Fowler notes he has seen this simple-sounding plan go down in flames most of the time. Rewrites stall because users keep demanding new features during a multi-year effort, and reproducing all the existing behavior, much of it unwanted, proves unexpectedly complex.

## The Strangler Approach

Instead, teams make small additions, often new features, built on top of yet separate from the legacy code base, and gradually shift behavior into the new system. This delivers reduced risk from small replacements, earlier return on investment, and organizational learning that informs later phases. Practitioners Cartwright, Horn and Lewis identify four key activities: align on desired outcomes, decompose into manageable pieces, deliver components successfully, and evolve organizational practices. The pattern accepts some transitional architecture, temporary bridge code, whose cost is repaid through lower risk and visible incremental value.

title: Martin Fowler, SacrificialArchitecture
text:
## Definition

Sacrificial architecture means deliberately accepting that the code you build today may be discarded in a few years. Fowler puts it directly: often the best code you can write now is code you will discard in a couple of years time. Throwing away a codebase is not a mark of failure but can be a sign of success, because it means the product grew beyond what the original architecture could support.

## The eBay Example

eBay began as Perl scripts built over a weekend in 1995, was completely rewritten in C++ in 1997, then rewritten again in Java in 2002. Fowler asks whether these early versions were errors because they were replaced, and answers: hardly. The right architecture to support 1996-era eBay was never going to be the right architecture for 2006-era eBay, because the traffic grew by orders of magnitude.

## Google's Rule of Thumb

Google institutionalizes the idea with Jeff Dean's guideline to design for roughly 10X growth but plan to rewrite before roughly 100X. Subsystems are routinely redesigned and discarded every few years rather than stretched past their design point.

## Tensions and Organizational Reality

Early systems should favor feature flexibility over raw performance, but sacrificing internal code quality backfires quickly, so good modularity still matters because clean module boundaries let you replace one component gracefully. Fowler warns that accounting practices, such as amortizing a codebase as a capital asset, can create pressure against retiring code that should be sacrificed, and that the team who built the sacrificial code should be the ones who decide when to sacrifice it.

title: Martin Fowler, Microservices and the First Law of Distributed Objects (Microservice Trade-Offs)
text:
## Benefits

Strong Module Boundaries: microservices reinforce modular structure because service boundaries are a hard barrier to references between modules, discouraging the workarounds that erode a monolith's internal structure as a team grows. Fowler ties this to Conway's Law and to decentralized data management, which eliminates the shared integration database and its coupling.

Independent Deployment: services can be deployed autonomously. If you mess one up you will not bring down the entire system, which supports continuous delivery and shortens the cycle time from idea to production.

Technology Diversity: each service can make its own technology choices, giving considerable freedom within a service and enabling gradual, service-by-service technology migration.

## Costs

Distribution: distributed systems are harder to program. Remote calls are slow, and if a service calls half a dozen remote services those response times add up. Remote calls can fail, so you need resilience patterns and asynchronous programming, both of which add cognitive load. This is the First Law of Distributed Objects: do not distribute your objects unless you must.

Eventual Consistency: decentralized data management means you cannot rely on distributed transactions, so there are windows where data is out of sync. Developers need to be aware of consistency issues and figure out how to detect when things are out of sync and how to reconcile them.

Operational Complexity: running many rapidly changing services demands a mature operations organization. Continuous delivery, monitoring, and a devops culture become essential rather than optional for a serious microservices setup, and a team without that operational maturity will struggle.

title: Martin Fowler, Conway's Law
text:
## The Original Law

Melvin Conway's 1968 observation is that any organization that designs a system will produce a design whose structure is a copy of the organization's communication structure. Fowler treats this not as a witticism but as a genuine force in software design.

## The Homomorphic Force

Software coupling is enabled and encouraged by human communication. Teams that communicate easily tend to produce tightly coupled code, while teams separated by floors, cities, or time zones tend to produce more loosely coupled systems. The architecture inevitably mirrors the org chart. Fowler's classic illustration: if you assign four groups to build a compiler, you get a four-pass compiler, because the system structure reflects the team structure.

## Three Responses to Conway's Law

You can ignore it, though it operates whether you acknowledge it or not. You can accept it and ensure your architecture aligns with your desired communication patterns. Or you can apply the Inverse Conway Maneuver: deliberately alter the development team's organization structure to encourage the software architecture you want, typically reorganizing teams around business capabilities rather than technical layers to encourage autonomous, independently deployable services.

## Key Insight

Fowler stresses that the modular decomposition of a system and the decomposition of the development organization must be done together, and must co-evolve over the life of the product. Ignoring Conway's Law is dangerous because a team structure that fights the desired architecture will keep pulling the design back toward the shape of the org chart.

title: Martin Fowler, MicroservicePrerequisites (You must be this tall)
text:
## You Must Be This Tall To Use Microservices

Fowler argues there is a set of baseline capabilities an organization needs before it should take on the complexity of microservices. Skipping them means the operational overhead of distribution will overwhelm the team.

## Rapid Provisioning

You should be able to fire up a new server in a matter of hours. This implies significant automation, though some manual steps are acceptable at first. It fits cloud infrastructure but does not strictly require it.

## Basic Monitoring

With many services in production you must detect failures fast. Fowler stresses monitoring both technical metrics (error rates, service availability) and business metrics (a drop in orders per minute), so you can catch and roll back bad changes quickly.

## Rapid Application Deployment

You need to deploy an application, to test or production, quickly, ideally within a couple of hours, typically via a deployment pipeline. Manual steps are tolerable at first but serious microservice operation needs full automation.

## DevOps Culture

You need close collaboration between developers and operations so that provisioning, deployment, and incident response are shared responsibilities, with both sides involved in problem resolution and root-cause analysis. Fowler notes these capabilities are good practice for a monolith too, and that scaling past a handful of services requires still more maturity, such as distributed tracing and continuous delivery.

title: Martin Fowler, Yagni (You Aren't Gonna Need It)
text:
## Definition

YAGNI, You Aren't Gonna Need It, is a principle from Extreme Programming: a capability you presume the software will need in the future should not be built now, because you aren't gonna need it. Build only what you currently need, not what you speculate about. Fowler frames the target as presumptive features, features you are putting in because you presume the system will need them later.

## The Four Costs of Building Presumptive Features

Cost of Build: all the effort spent analyzing, programming, and testing a feature that turns out not to be needed, or not needed in the form you built.

Cost of Delay: building the presumptive feature now uses capacity you could have spent on features that are needed now, delaying real revenue and learning.

Cost of Carry: the presumptive feature's code adds complexity to the system, making every other change harder, and this drag lasts for the whole time the code sits there unused.

Cost of Repair: when you finally do build the real feature, your earlier guess is usually wrong, so you must rework it, and you often would have been better off starting fresh.

## Critical Distinction and Caveat

YAGNI applies only to presumptive features, not to the effort that makes software easier to change, such as refactoring, good modularity, testing, and continuous delivery. Those enabling practices are what make YAGNI safe, because they let you add the feature cheaply later. Fowler is emphatic that Yagni is not a justification for neglecting the health of your code base: skimping on internal quality is not YAGNI, it is just poor engineering.

title: Simon Brown, The C4 Model for Visualising Software Architecture
text:
## A Map of Your Code at Different Zoom Levels

Simon Brown's C4 model is a way to describe and communicate software architecture using a set of hierarchical diagrams, like Google Maps zooming from continents down to streets. It is easy to learn, developer friendly, and both notation independent and tooling independent. The name comes from the four levels: Context, Containers, Components, and Code.

## The Core Abstractions

C4 builds on a small vocabulary. A software system is the highest level of abstraction, delivering value to users. A container is a separately runnable or deployable unit that executes code or stores data, such as a server-side web application, single-page app, mobile app, database, or file system (note: not a Docker container). A component is a grouping of related functionality behind a well-defined interface. A person is a human user of the system.

## The Four Levels

Level 1, System Context diagram: shows your software system as a single box in the middle, surrounded by its users and the other systems it interacts with. Audience: everyone, technical and non-technical.

Level 2, Container diagram: zooms into the system boundary to show the high-level technical building blocks (the containers) and how responsibilities are distributed, plus the major technology choices and how containers communicate. Audience: technical people inside and outside the team.

Level 3, Component diagram: zooms into an individual container to show the components inside it and their responsibilities and technology details. Audience: architects and developers.

Level 4, Code diagram: an optional zoom into a component to show how it is implemented, using UML class diagrams or entity relationship diagrams. Usually best generated on demand by tooling rather than drawn by hand.

## Notation Guidance

C4 does not prescribe a specific notation, but every element should be self-describing: give each box a name, an element type (person, system, container, or component), a technology where relevant, and a short description, and label every relationship with its purpose and, ideally, protocol. Supplementary diagrams include system landscape, dynamic, and deployment views.

title: Michael Nygard, Documenting Architecture Decisions (the original ADR)
text:
## The Problem

Michael Nygard's original article introduces the Architecture Decision Record. He identifies two failure modes. First, lost context: new team members confront existing architecture decisions with no record of why they were made, so they either accept them blindly (perhaps keeping an outdated decision) or reverse them blindly (perhaps breaking a non-functional requirement). Second, documentation decay: large architecture documents go unread and become obsolete. He notes that most developers have been on a project where the specification document was larger in bytes than the total source code.

## Architecturally Significant Decisions

An architecturally significant decision is one that affects the structure, non-functional characteristics, dependencies, interfaces, or construction techniques of the system. These are the decisions worth recording.

## The ADR Format

Nygard proposes capturing each decision in a short text file with a numbered sequence, using these sections. Title: a short noun phrase, for example ADR 1: Deployment on Ruby on Rails 3.0.10. Context: a value-neutral description of the forces at play, including technological, political, social, and project-local forces, often in tension. Decision: the response to those forces, stated in active voice, We will. Status: proposed, accepted, deprecated, or superseded, with references to any superseding ADR. Consequences: the resulting context after applying the decision, all of it, positive, negative, and neutral, since consequences affect the team going forward.

## Implementation Guidance

Keep each ADR one or two pages, written as a conversation with a future developer, using full sentences. Store them in version control alongside the code, for example doc/arch/adr-NNN.md. Number sequentially and never reuse a number. Crucially, do not delete or edit a reversed decision: keep the record and mark it superseded, so the history of the thinking is preserved.

title: Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, Team Topologies Key Concepts
text:
## The Team As The Fundamental Means Of Delivery

Team Topologies, by Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, argues that the team, not the individual, is the fundamental means of software delivery, and that organizations should be designed for a fast flow of change. It provides a thinking model rather than a fixed org chart, and it uses the Inverse Conway Maneuver to shape team structure so the desired architecture emerges.

## Four Fundamental Team Types

Stream-aligned team: aligned to a single valuable flow of work, usually a segment of the business domain, and able to deliver that flow without waiting on others. This is the primary team type; the others exist to support it.

Enabling team: helps stream-aligned teams overcome obstacles and detects missing capabilities, acting as mentors who raise the capability of others rather than doing the work for them.

Complicated-subsystem team: owns a part of the system that needs significant mathematics, calculation, or deep technical expertise, so that specialist knowledge is not spread thin across many teams.

Platform team: provides a compelling internal product, a platform, that accelerates delivery by stream-aligned teams by hiding underlying complexity behind self-service interfaces.

## Three Team Interaction Modes

Collaboration: two teams work closely together for a defined period to discover new things such as APIs, practices, or technologies, accepting higher overhead in exchange for rapid learning.

X-as-a-Service: one team consumes something, such as an API or platform, that another team provides as a service, with minimal collaboration, which is best when responsibilities are clear.

Facilitating: one team helps and mentors another to remove impediments, the mode an enabling team typically uses.

## Team Cognitive Load

A central constraint is team cognitive load. A team can only own as much software as it can hold in its collective head; overloaded teams slow down and make poor decisions. You limit cognitive load by giving a team a bounded, well-matched responsibility, which is why team boundaries should align with clear domain boundaries.

title: Adam Wiggins et al., The Twelve-Factor App
text:
## Purpose

The Twelve-Factor App is a methodology, originally from Heroku, for building software-as-a-service apps that are portable, deployable to modern cloud platforms, and scalable without significant rearchitecting. A technical lead uses it as a checklist for operational fitness.

## The Twelve Factors

I. Codebase: one codebase tracked in revision control, many deploys. One-to-one relationship between codebase and app.

II. Dependencies: explicitly declare and isolate dependencies. Never rely on implicit system-wide packages.

III. Config: store config in the environment. Strictly separate config, which varies between deploys, from code, which does not.

IV. Backing services: treat backing services (databases, queues, caches, SMTP) as attached resources, accessed by a URL or config, swappable without code changes.

V. Build, release, run: strictly separate the build stage, the release stage, and the run stage. Releases are immutable and every release has a unique id.

VI. Processes: execute the app as one or more stateless processes. Any persistent data must live in a backing service; never rely on sticky sessions or local memory.

VII. Port binding: export services via port binding. The app is self-contained and binds to a port rather than relying on runtime injection of a webserver.

VIII. Concurrency: scale out via the process model. Handle diverse workloads by running more processes of appropriate types rather than making one process bigger.

IX. Disposability: maximize robustness with fast startup and graceful shutdown, so processes can be started or stopped at a moment's notice, aiding elastic scaling and resilient deploys.

X. Dev/prod parity: keep development, staging, and production as similar as possible, minimizing gaps in time, personnel, and tools to enable continuous deployment.

XI. Logs: treat logs as event streams. The app never manages log files; it writes to stdout and the execution environment routes the stream.

XII. Admin processes: run admin and management tasks (migrations, one-off scripts) as one-off processes in an identical environment to the app's long-running processes.

title: Martin Fowler, BoundedContext (Domain-Driven Design)
text:
## Definition

Bounded Context is a central pattern in Domain-Driven Design, from Eric Evans's book. DDD deals with large models by dividing them into different bounded contexts and being explicit about their interrelationships. A bounded context is an explicit boundary within which a particular domain model applies.

## The Central Problem

A total unification of the domain model for a large system will not be feasible or cost-effective. As an organization grows, different departments use subtly different vocabularies for what look like the same concepts. Terms such as Customer and Product mean different things in a sales context than in a support context; the sales model and the support model may share the word but carry different attributes and behavior.

## The Polysemy Example

Fowler gives an electricity utility example where the term meter had distinct meanings: the connection between the grid and a location, the grid and a customer, and the physical meter device itself. These distinctions could be smoothed over in conversation but not in the precise world of computers, so forcing one shared model creates confusion and bugs.

## Ubiquitous Language and Context Mapping

A model acts as a Ubiquitous Language shared between developers and domain experts, but that language is only valid within a single bounded context. Different contexts may have completely different models of a common concept. DDD strategic design uses a Context Map to describe the relationships between bounded contexts and the mechanisms used to translate, or map, between the polysemic concepts for integration. Aligning bounded contexts with team boundaries is a direct application of Conway's Law.

title: Thoughtworks, Fitness-function-driven development (Evolutionary Architecture)
text:
## Evolutionary Architecture

The idea, from Neal Ford, Rebecca Parsons, Patrick Kua and colleagues, is that an evolutionary architecture supports guided, incremental change as the first principle across multiple dimensions. Rather than fixing the architecture up front and hoping it survives, you build in mechanisms that let it change safely over time.

## Architectural Fitness Functions

A fitness function describes how close an architecture is to achieving an architectural aim, and provides an objective integrity assessment of some architectural characteristic. Just as test-driven development verifies business outcomes with tests, fitness functions verify architectural characteristics such as scalability, reliability, observability, security, performance, and coupling. They give continuous feedback on architectural conformance during development rather than only after deployment.

## Categories

Fitness functions span many dimensions: code quality (test coverage, maintainability), resiliency (error rates and latency tolerance during deployments), observability (logging, metrics, tracing), performance (transaction times and throughput under load), security (vulnerability and secrets scanning), compliance (PII protection, audit requirements), and operability (runbooks, alerting). In the broader evolutionary-architecture framing they are also classified as atomic versus holistic, triggered versus continuous, and automated versus manual.

## Guardrails Against Drift

Fitness functions act as automated gatekeepers within the delivery pipeline, catching unmaintainable or non-compliant changes before they reach production while not blocking the flow to production. They help teams avoid architectural drift and objectively measure technical debt, notifying the team quickly when the code diverges from the intended architecture.

title: ScyllaDB Glossary, CAP Theorem
text:
## The Theorem

Eric Brewer's CAP theorem states that a distributed data store can simultaneously provide only two of three guarantees: Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance. It is a foundational trade-off every technical lead designing distributed systems must reason about.

## The Three Guarantees

Consistency: all clients see the same data at the same time regardless of which node they connect to; a read receives the most recent write or an error. Achieving it requires writes to be reflected across nodes before a read is served.

Availability: any client making a request receives a valid, non-error response, even when some nodes are down, but there is no guarantee it reflects the most recent write.

Partition tolerance: the system continues to operate despite a partition, which is a break in communications, a temporarily delayed or lost connection between nodes.

## The Practical Trade-Off

Because network failures are inevitable in a real distributed system, partition tolerance is not optional. That reduces the real choice, during a partition, to two stances. A CP system (consistency plus partition tolerance) sacrifices availability: it refuses or blocks requests on nodes that cannot be made consistent until the partition heals; examples cited include MongoDB and Redis. An AP system (availability plus partition tolerance) sacrifices consistency: nodes stay available but may return stale data; examples cited include Cassandra, CouchDB, and ScyllaDB. A truly CA distributed database does not exist in practice because partitions cannot be prevented.

## PACELC Extension

PACELC extends CAP by noting that even when the system is running normally, with no partition (the Else case), there is still a trade-off between latency and consistency, which CAP alone does not capture.

title: Will Larson, StaffEng: Staff Engineer Archetypes
text:
## The Four Archetypes

Will Larson, in StaffEng, observes that the Staff-plus engineer role is not one job but several, and names four archetypes so that engineers and managers can talk concretely about the work.

Tech Lead: guides the approach and execution of a particular team, and partners closely with a single manager, sometimes across a small cluster of teams. This is the most common archetype and is the closest to day-to-day team delivery.

Architect: responsible for the direction, quality, and approach within a critical area. Architects combine deep technical knowledge, broad context, and strong, well-argued opinions to steer how a domain is built, and they earn that role through demonstrated judgment rather than title.

Solver: digs deep into arbitrarily complex problems and finds an appropriate path forward. The Solver is a trusted troubleshooter that leadership points at the most important or gnarly problem of the moment, then redirects to the next one once it is handled.

Right Hand: extends an executive's attention by borrowing their scope and authority to operate a particularly complex part of the organization. This is the rarest archetype and appears only in large organizations, functioning as a senior leader without direct managerial reports.

## Why Archetypes Matter

Larson notes that which archetypes exist depends on company culture and scale: Tech Lead roles appear early in team-oriented organizations, Solver roles thrive where individual heroics are valued, and Architect and Right Hand roles tend to emerge only as organizations scale into the hundreds and then thousands of engineers. Knowing your archetype clarifies what work to seek and how you will be evaluated.

title: Martin Fowler, Who Needs an Architect? (IEEE Software)
text:
## What Is Architecture

Fowler opens with a colleague, Dave Rice, saying we shouldn't interview anyone who has architect on his resume, capturing the contempt many good engineers feel for the smug, self-important sense of the word. Fowler then quotes Ralph Johnson: in most successful software projects, the expert developers working on that project have a shared understanding of the system design, and this shared understanding is called architecture. It includes how the system is divided into components and how the components interact through interfaces. Architecture is the highest level concept of the expert developers, and what makes a component significant is that the expert developers say so. Architecture is therefore a social construct, about what parts of the software are considered important by group consensus.

## The Two Architect Archetypes

Architectus Reloadus is the person who makes all the important decisions, on the grounds that a single mind is needed to ensure conceptual integrity, and often because the architect does not think the team members are skilled enough to make those decisions. These decisions are made early so everyone else has a plan to follow. This is the ivory-tower, Matrix Reloaded species of architect Fowler distrusts.

Architectus Oryzus is a different animal: an architect who is deeply aware of what is going on in the project, who pairs and programs with developers in the morning and joins a requirements session in the afternoon to explain the technical consequences of ideas in non-technical terms such as development cost. The most important activity of this architect is to mentor the development team, to raise their level so they can take on more complex issues themselves. Mike Two named this role guide, as in mountaineering. This yields the satisfying rule of thumb that an architect's value is inversely proportional to the number of decisions he or she makes.

## Getting Rid of Software Architecture

Fowler recalls Johnson's secondary definition: architecture is the decisions that you wish you could get right early in a project. People end up defining architecture as the things that people perceive as hard to change. It is commonly believed a database schema must be right early because it is hard to change once live, but Pramod Sadalage devised evolutionary database techniques that made the schema no longer architectural. Citing Enrico Zaninotto, Fowler notes that irreversibility is one of the prime drivers of complexity, so one of an architect's most important tasks is to remove architecture by finding ways to eliminate irreversibility in software designs. Johnson adds that making everything easy to change makes the entire system very complex, because complexity, and duplication, are what make software hard to change. Fowler ends: we have met the enemy, and he is us.

title: Fallacies of Distributed Computing (Deutsch, Gosling, Sun Microsystems)
text:
## The Eight Fallacies

The Fallacies of Distributed Computing are a set of false assumptions that programmers new to distributed applications invariably make. They were assembled largely by L. Peter Deutsch and others at Sun Microsystems, with James Gosling adding the eighth around 1997. A technical lead designing any networked or microservices system should treat every one of these as false.

The eight fallacies are: 1. The network is reliable. 2. Latency is zero. 3. Bandwidth is infinite. 4. The network is secure. 5. Topology doesn't change. 6. There is one administrator. 7. Transport cost is zero. 8. The network is homogeneous.

## Why They Matter

Assuming these statements are true leads directly to broken systems. Treating the network as reliable produces code with no retry, timeout, or failure handling. Assuming zero latency and infinite bandwidth produces chatty designs that collapse under real round-trip times and payload sizes. Assuming the network is secure ignores encryption, authentication, and untrusted intermediaries. Assuming a fixed topology and a single administrator ignores that nodes move, addresses change, and many parties operate the infrastructure. Assuming zero transport cost and a homogeneous network ignores serialization overhead and the reality of mixed hardware, protocols, and versions. The practical consequence is that distributed systems must be designed defensively, with error handling, backpressure, idempotency, and observability built in from the start, because the network will violate every one of these assumptions.

title: Jeff Bezos, Amazon 2015 Letter to Shareholders (Type 1 vs Type 2 Decisions)
text:
## One-Size-Fits-All Decision Making Is A Trap

Bezos frames a common pitfall for large organizations, one that hurts speed and inventiveness: one-size-fits-all decision making. The remedy is to recognize that not all decisions carry the same weight and should not use the same process.

## Type 1 and Type 2 Decisions

Some decisions are consequential and irreversible or nearly irreversible, one-way doors, and these decisions must be made methodically, carefully, slowly, with great deliberation and consultation. If you walk through and don't like what you see on the other side, you can't get back to where you were before. Bezos calls these Type 1 decisions.

But most decisions aren't like that, they are changeable, reversible, they are two-way doors. If you've made a suboptimal Type 2 decision, you don't have to live with the consequences for that long. You can reopen the door and go back through. Type 2 decisions can and should be made quickly by high judgment individuals or small groups.

## The Failure Mode At Scale

As organizations get larger, there seems to be a tendency to use the heavy-weight Type 1 decision-making process on most decisions, including many Type 2 decisions. The end result of this is slowness, unthoughtful risk aversion, failure to experiment sufficiently, and consequently diminished invention. Bezos notes in a footnote that the opposite error, habitually using the light-weight Type 2 process to make Type 1 decisions, tends to make companies go extinct before they get large, so there is survivorship bias in only seeing the first failure mode. For a technical lead, the lesson is to spend deliberation budget on the truly irreversible architectural choices and move fast on the reversible ones.

title: Jeff Bezos, Amazon 2016 Letter to Shareholders (High-Velocity Decision Making)
text:
## Day 1 Versus Day 2

Bezos warns that Day 2 is stasis, followed by irrelevance, followed by excruciating, painful decline, followed by death, which is why staying in Day 1 requires deliberate practices. One of the keys is high-quality, high-velocity decision making, because slow decision making corrodes a company as surely as bad decisions.

## Four Practices For High-Velocity Decisions

First, never use a one-size-fits-all decision-making process. Many decisions are reversible, two-way doors, and those decisions can use a light-weight process, so you do not need to treat every choice as if it were irreversible.

Second, most decisions should probably be made with somewhere around 70 percent of the information you wish you had. If you wait for 90 percent, in most cases you are probably being slow, and either way you need to be good at quickly recognizing and correcting bad decisions.

Third, use the phrase disagree and commit: if you have conviction on a direction even though there is no consensus, it is helpful to say, look, I know we disagree on this but will you gamble with me on it? This is not one-way; if you are the senior leader you should also be willing to disagree and commit when your team feels strongly. Bezos gives the example of green-lighting an Amazon Studios original by telling the team he disagreed but was willing to roll the dice with them.

Fourth, recognize true misalignment issues early and escalate them immediately, rather than letting disputes drag on and be resolved by whoever has more stamina, which is exhausting and yields a random rather than a thoughtful answer. Together these tactics preserve the energy and dynamism of Day 1 at large scale.

title: Fred Brooks, The Second-System Effect (The Mythical Man-Month)
text:
## The Anti-Pattern

The second-system effect, coined by Fred Brooks in The Mythical Man-Month based on IBM's move from simpler operating systems to the ambitious OS/360, describes the tendency of a successful first system, often small and relatively elegant, to be followed by a second system that becomes over-engineered or bloated. It is a classic trap for a newly promoted architect or technical lead.

## Why The Second System Is The Most Dangerous

Brooks argues the second system is the most dangerous system a person ever designs. On the first system the designer is cautious, knowing they are on unfamiliar ground, so the result tends to be spare and clean. Flush with the success of the first, and now overconfident, the designer is tempted to incorporate every previously deferred improvement, optional feature, and generalization all at once. The resulting successor is harder to build, harder to understand, and harder to evolve, and it often carries features tuned to a past era that no longer matter.

## Guarding Against It

Brooks recommends explicit discipline: resist functional ornamentation and unnecessary generalization, make the resource cost of each small feature visible so its true price is weighed, and ensure architectural leadership from designers who have already been through more than one system and learned self-restraint. Modern practice adds staged delivery, strict scope management, prioritizing validated over speculative requirements, and architectural reviews that specifically challenge speculative features. The through-line with YAGNI and the technical debt quadrant is that discipline about what not to build is as important as skill in building.

title: Malte Ubl, Design Docs at Google
text:
## What A Design Doc Is

Malte Ubl describes the design doc as the most important tool for gaining and documenting design context at Google. It is an informal document that the author or team writes before starting a major software project. It documents the high level implementation strategy and key design decisions, with emphasis on the trade-offs that were considered during those decisions. The core insight is that as software engineers our job is not to produce code per se, but to solve problems, and unstructured text like a doc is a better early tool than code for that.

## Why They Are Worth It

The primary value is in the process, not the artifact. Writing and reviewing a design doc identifies design issues early when change is cheap, achieves consensus around an approach, ensures cross-cutting concerns such as security, privacy, and observability are actually considered, scales the knowledge of senior engineers across the org, and creates organizational memory of design rationale.

## Typical Anatomy

Context and Scope: a short, objective, value-neutral overview of the landscape and what is being built. Goals and Non-Goals: bullet lists that state the actual objectives and, importantly, what is deliberately out of scope. The Actual Design: begins with an overview and goes into detail, emphasizing trade-offs, often including a system-context-diagram, API sketches (not full formal definitions), and the data storage approach, while rarely including code or pseudocode. Alternatives Considered: competing designs and their trade-offs, explaining why the chosen one best meets the goals. Cross-cutting Concerns: dedicated sections for security, privacy, observability, and org-specific concerns.

## When To Write One, And When Not

Write a design doc when the right design is uncertain or contentious, when senior involvement would help, or when the team tends to overlook cross-cutting concerns. Do not write one when the solution is obvious with no significant trade-offs, or when it would degrade into a mere implementation manual. Length is typically ten to twenty pages for large projects, or a one to three page mini design doc for smaller work. The decision is a cost-benefit trade-off: docs save money by avoiding coding rabbit holes, and cost money because writing and review take time.

title: AWS Well-Architected Framework, The Six Pillars (Definitions)
text:
## The Six Pillars

The AWS Well-Architected Framework gives a technical lead a consistent set of best practices and a set of questions to evaluate how well an architecture aligns with them. It rests on six pillars, and architecting is largely about making conscious trade-offs between them based on business context.

Operational excellence: the ability to support development and run workloads effectively, gain insight into their operations, and continuously improve supporting processes and procedures to deliver business value.

Security: how to take advantage of cloud technologies to protect data, systems, and assets in a way that can improve your security posture.

Reliability: the ability of a workload to perform its intended function correctly and consistently when it is expected to, including the ability to operate and test the workload through its total lifecycle.

Performance efficiency: the ability to use computing resources efficiently to meet system requirements, and to maintain that efficiency as demand changes and technologies evolve.

Cost optimization: the ability to run systems to deliver business value at the lowest price point.

Sustainability: the ability to continually improve sustainability impacts by reducing energy consumption and increasing efficiency across all components of a workload, maximizing the benefit from provisioned resources and minimizing the total resources required.

## Key Terms And Trade-Offs

AWS defines a component as the code, configuration, and resources that together deliver against a requirement, and usually the unit of technical ownership. A workload is a set of components that together deliver business value and is the level at which business and technology leaders communicate. Architecture is how components work together in a workload. When architecting, you make trade-offs between pillars: you might trade reliability for lower cost and sustainability impact in development environments, or accept higher cost and sustainability impact to maximize reliability for mission-critical solutions. Notably, AWS says security and operational excellence are generally not traded off against the other pillars.

title: Fred Brooks, No Silver Bullet: Essence and Accidents of Software Engineering
text:
## The Central Claim

Fred Brooks's essay argues that there is no single development, in either technology or management technique, which by itself promises even one order of magnitude, a tenfold, improvement within a decade in productivity, in reliability, or in simplicity. This is a permanent warning to technical leads against silver-bullet thinking, the belief that some new language, framework, or methodology will by itself transform delivery.

## Essence Versus Accidents

Brooks divides the difficulties of software into essence and accidents. Accidental complexity refers to difficulties that attend the production of software but are not inherent, problems engineers themselves create and can therefore solve, such as awkward assembly language or slow batch turnaround, much of which better languages and tools have already removed. Essential complexity is the complexity inherent in the nature of the software problem itself, and it cannot be abstracted away: if the users need a program to do thirty different things, those thirty things are essential, and the program must do them.

## The Four Essential Properties

Brooks attributes essential difficulty to four properties of software's nature: complexity (software entities are more complex for their size than perhaps any other human construct, and this complexity is essential not incidental), conformity (software must conform to the many arbitrary interfaces and institutions it is forced to join), changeability (software is constantly pressured to change because it is malleable and embodies function, which is the most subject to change), and invisibility (software is not embedded in space and has no ready geometric representation, so it resists visualization).

## The Implication

Because past productivity gains mostly attacked accidental complexity, and that well is running dry, future order-of-magnitude gains would have to attack the essence, which is far harder. Brooks's promising directions are not a single tool but a set of disciplines: buy versus build rather than write software that already exists, rapid prototyping to nail down requirements, growing software organically through incremental development rather than building it all at once, and above all identifying, developing, and rewarding great designers, since the difference between great and ordinary designers can be an order of magnitude by itself.

title: Brian Foote and Joseph Yoder, Big Ball of Mud
text:
## The Anti-Pattern

Foote and Yoder define a Big Ball of Mud as a casually, even haphazardly, structured system whose organization, if one can call it that, is dictated more by expediency than design. It is a haphazardly structured, sprawling, sloppy, duct-tape-and-baling-wire, spaghetti-code jungle, showing the unmistakable signs of unregulated growth and repeated, expedient repair, with promiscuous information sharing and the erosion of whatever structure it once had. Bluntly, they call it the de-facto standard software architecture, the most frequently deployed of all, which is precisely why a technical lead must understand the forces that produce it.

## The Forces That Produce Mud

The authors argue mud is not produced by incompetence but by real forces that consistently override architectural concern: Time (deadline pressure, since architecture's payoff comes too late), Cost (good architecture needs premium skill and upfront investment whose returns arrive slowly), Experience and Skill (domain inexperience and wide variance in programmer ability), Visibility (architecture is under the hood and invisible to stakeholders who only see a working system), Complexity (software reflects essential domain complexity), Change (unpredictable requirement shifts cut across the original design), and Scale (managing large systems is qualitatively, not just quantitatively, harder). Understanding these forces means you fight mud with process and refactoring, not by blaming developers.

## Related Patterns

The paper names patterns that describe how mud forms and how to fight it. Throwaway Code: quick disposable code for a prototype that often takes on a life of its own, the problem being that throwaway code comes when it is not thrown away. Piecemeal Growth: incrementally address the forces that encourage change and growth, exploit growth opportunities locally as they occur, and refactor unrelentingly. Keep It Working: do what it takes to keep the software running, via daily builds and rigorous testing, so you always have fast feedback. Shearing Layers: factor the system so artifacts that change at similar rates live together, separating fast-changing from stable elements. Sweeping It Under the Rug: if you cannot make a mess go away, at least cordon it off behind a facade so the disorder is localized. Reconstruction: when decline is irreversible, throw it away and start over. These give a technical lead a vocabulary for both preventing and rehabilitating mud.

title: Gremlin, Is Your Microservice a Distributed Monolith?
text:
## The Anti-Pattern

A distributed monolith is an application that is deployed like a microservice but is built like a monolith. It runs on distributed platforms such as Kubernetes yet lacks the architectural independence that makes microservices worthwhile, so it combines the heaviness and inflexibility of monoliths, the complexity of microservices, and few of the benefits of either architecture. It is the classic worst-of-both-worlds outcome a technical lead must watch for after a naive decomposition.

## The Tell-Tale Signs

Tight coupling: services exhibit behavioral, temporal, or implementation coupling, so they depend on one another being available and responsive, and failures cascade from one container to the next. Changes to one service force changes across several others, which means you have lost independent deployment and services effectively release in lock-step. Poor scalability: scaling horizontally is inefficient because the system was not designed for distributed deployment, so you must scale whole application instances rather than individual services, wasting resources. Excessive inter-service communication: the services are overly chatty, making extensive synchronous API calls, so network latency between tightly integrated services becomes a critical bottleneck that can cause timeouts and other unexpected failures. A shared database that several services read and write is another implicit coupling that turns independent services into a single unit.

## Why It Happens And How To Catch It

The anti-pattern emerges from inadequate service-boundary definition and insufficient architectural planning before a migration, when teams repackage monolithic logic into containers without redesigning for distributed independence, essentially creating a monolith packaged as a microservice. This is the practical realization of Fowler's warning in MonolithFirst that getting service boundaries wrong is worse than not splitting at all. Gremlin recommends using chaos engineering to validate resilience, injecting failures such as blackhole and latency attacks to observe whether services degrade gracefully or cascade, and stress-testing scaling and response-time degradation under adverse network conditions, so that hidden coupling is exposed before production does it for you.
